name: Deductive Reasoning
description: Drawing valid inferences where the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion — applying rules of inference such as modus ponens, modus tollens, and hypothetical syllogism to produce necessarily truth-preserving arguments

steps.name: Establish Premises — Identify and state all propositions accepted as true
steps.description: Identify and clearly state every premise of the argument. Per Wikipedia, deductive reasoning 'starts from the premises and reasons to a conclusion based on and supported by these premises.' Premises may be universal generalizations (all A are B), conditional statements (if P then Q), or established facts. Distinguish between premises that are self-evident axioms, empirically verified truths, and assumed propositions. Each premise must be stated unambiguously so its logical form can be analyzed in the next step.

SearchMemories.reason: Find established principles, axioms, and known truths in the relevant domain that can serve as premises

BuildContext.reason: Understand relationships between candidate premises and their domain of applicability

stop_conditions: All premises identified and stated as clear propositions
Each premise classified by epistemic status: axiom, empirical truth, or assumption
Premises stated unambiguously with identifiable logical connectives (if-then, all-are, etc.)
Domain and scope of applicability established for each premise

steps.name: Analyze Logical Form — Determine the syntactic structure of the argument
steps.description:
Determine the logical form of the argument. Per Wikipedia's syntactic approach, 'whether an argument is deductively valid depends only on its form, syntax, or structure.' Two arguments have the same form if they use the same logical vocabulary in the same arrangement, even if their contents differ. Classify the argument structure: Is it a conditional (P→Q)? A categorical syllogism (All A are B, all B are C)? A disjunction (P∨Q)? Express the argument abstractly to make the common syntax explicit — e.g., 'if A then B; A; therefore B.' Identify which rule of inference the argument follows or should follow.

🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Map each premise to its formal structure. Identify the logical connectives (→, ∧, ∨, ¬, ∀, ∃). Determine whether the argument pattern matches a known valid form (modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunction elimination) or might be a formal fallacy (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent).

SequentialThinking.reason: Translating natural-language premises into formal logical structure requires careful step-by-step analysis of connectives, quantifiers, and argument patterns — per Wikipedia, 'it is usually necessary to express the argument in a formal language in order to assess whether it is valid'

BuildContext.reason: Check for known argument forms and logical patterns in the knowledge graph

stop_conditions: Each premise expressed in formal logical notation with identified connectives
Argument pattern classified (conditional, syllogistic, disjunctive, etc.)
Candidate rule of inference identified (modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, etc.)
Potential formal fallacy patterns flagged for screening in later steps
next_actions: Proceed to applying rules of inference

steps.name: Apply Rules of Inference — Construct the deductive inference chain
steps.description:
Apply valid rules of inference to derive conclusions from premises. Per Wikipedia, this is the core deductive operation. The primary rules are:

• Modus ponens (affirming the antecedent): P→Q, P ∴ Q — 'the primary deductive rule of inference'
• Modus tollens (law of contrapositive): P→Q, ¬Q ∴ ¬P — reasoning goes opposite direction to conditional
• Hypothetical syllogism: P→Q, Q→R ∴ P→R — chains conditional statements
• Disjunction elimination: P∨Q, ¬P ∴ Q

Per Wikipedia's distinction between definitory and strategic rules: definitory rules determine validity, while strategic rules guide which inferences to draw to reach the intended conclusion. Master both — select the right rule of inference and apply it correctly.

🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

For each inference step: state the rule being applied, show the premises consumed, and derive the intermediate or final conclusion. Ensure each step follows logically from the previous via a named rule of inference. Chain multiple inferences if needed to reach the target conclusion.

SequentialThinking.reason: Constructing valid inference chains via modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, and other rules requires rigorous step-by-step logical progression — each thought documents one inference step with its rule, premises, and derived conclusion

BuildContext.reason: Verify logical relationships and check for known counterexamples to intermediate conclusions

stop_conditions: Each inference step names the rule of inference applied (modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, etc.)
Each step shows which premises or intermediate conclusions are consumed
The inference chain connects premises to conclusion without gaps
Both definitory correctness (valid rule applied) and strategic appropriateness (right rule chosen) confirmed

steps.name: Derive Conclusion — State what necessarily follows from the premises
steps.description: State the conclusion that necessarily follows from the premises through the inference chain. Per Wikipedia, logical consequence has three essential features (Tarski): it is (1) necessary — the premises necessitate the conclusion, (2) formal — it depends only on form, not content, and (3) knowable a priori — no empirical investigation needed to determine validity. The conclusion must be stated with logical necessity, not mere probability — this is what distinguishes deductive from ampliative (inductive/abductive) reasoning. Per Wikipedia: 'the conclusion only repeats information already found in the premises' at the depth level, but may present it 'in a new and sometimes surprising way' at the surface level.

WriteMemory.reason: Document derived conclusions with their complete logical derivation chain for institutional memory

stop_conditions: Conclusion stated as a necessary consequence of premises — not merely probable
Scope of conclusion matches scope of premises (no overreach beyond what premises support)
Conclusion distinguished from ampliative inference — it is truth-preserving, not merely likely
Surface-level new information made explicit even though depth-level content was in premises
next_actions: Proceed to validity and soundness assessment

steps.name: Assess Validity and Soundness — Verify the argument is both valid and sound
steps.description:
Verify the argument's validity and soundness. Per Wikipedia, these are distinct properties: 'An argument is valid if it is impossible for its premises to be true while its conclusion is false. An argument is sound if it is valid and the premises are true.' Check validity via both approaches:

• Syntactic: Does each step follow a valid rule of inference? Are there any formal fallacies?
• Semantic: Is there any possible interpretation where premises are true and conclusion is false?

Screen explicitly for formal fallacies that Wikipedia identifies as commonly confused with valid forms:
• Affirming the consequent (P→Q, Q ∴ P) — resembles modus ponens
• Denying the antecedent (P→Q, ¬P ∴ ¬Q) — resembles modus tollens
• Affirming a disjunct, Denying a conjunct, Fallacy of the undistributed middle

Then check soundness: are all premises actually true? Per Wikipedia, 'it is possible to have a deductive argument that is logically valid but is not sound.'

🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

For each step in the inference chain: (1) verify formal validity, (2) screen for fallacy patterns, (3) check premise truth. Conclude with overall assessment: valid? sound? If unsound, identify which premises are questionable.

SequentialThinking.reason: Assessing both validity (formal structure) and soundness (premise truth) requires systematic checking of each inference step for formal fallacies and each premise for truth — per Wikipedia, 'even arguments with wrong premises can be deductively valid'

SearchMemories.reason: Search for known counterexamples, edge cases, or contradicting evidence that might challenge premise truth or reveal hidden formal fallacies

stop_conditions: Validity confirmed: each inference step follows a named valid rule of inference (syntactic check)
No formal fallacies detected: affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, undistributed middle, etc. all screened
Semantic check: no possible interpretation found where premises are true and conclusion is false
Soundness assessed: each premise evaluated for truth — argument classified as valid-and-sound or valid-but-unsound
If unsound, specific questionable premises identified with justification
next_actions: Document validated argument with proof chain and soundness assessment
